expectations.text: Recommended approach commits to one concrete direction (not 'it depends') and the Tradeoffs section names what gets worse under it
expectations.evidence: proposal.md Section 1 gives an unhedged, numbered decision: 'Stop investing in skills.sh as an installer... Adopt the standard flow for everything that leaves the dev machine... Add a one-file Claude Code marketplace... keep the monorepo... version numbers... implicit by default.' Sections 4 and 5 each open with an explicit 'Decision:' line. Downsides of that direction are explicitly named, not hand-waved: Section 5 states 'Trade-off accepted: with SHA-derived versions and source: "./", every commit re-versions every plugin and each plugin copy is the whole repo, so auto-updating installs re-copy on unrelated commits'; Section 4 states 'What you give up: control over conventions you were not exercising (no versions, no tags exist today), and acceptance of two third-party roadmaps.' Section 8's guardrails table adds further concrete costs (e.g., cache churn, no rollback on npx updates).

expectations.text: Every review trigger is falsifiable: contains a measurable threshold, count, or date
expectations.evidence: Section 9 'Triggers to revisit this decision' lists 5 triggers. Only one has a measurable threshold/count: 'The repo passes ~20 plugins or commits become daily -> explicit versions to stop cache churn.' The other four are qualitative/event-based with no threshold, count, or date: 'An external user... asks "which version am I on?"', 'A skill becomes a dependency of another plugin', 'Either ecosystem changes its discovery/layout conventions... re-evaluate then, not pre-emptively', and 'You want the Linear hooks on other machines.' These closely resemble the multi-agent-council skill's own documented bad-trigger pattern ('If things change significantly' / 'If the team feels it's not working' in references/proposal-document.md) rather than its good-trigger pattern (specific numeric thresholds). Since only 1 of 5 triggers is genuinely falsifiable by a measurable threshold/count/date, 'every review trigger' does not hold.

suggestions.assertion: proposal.md exists and contains all 7 required Proposal Document sections...
suggestions.reason: This run has 6 of 7 concepts clearly present with strong, well-cited content (Dissenting perspectives, Implementation scope and Review triggers are exemplary and even reuse the template's exact heading names) and fails only because there is no dedicated Problem/Goal framing -- the decision is stated in a header-table row but context/stakes are never established as their own unit. The all-or-nothing phrasing means a near-miss on one section grades identically to a proposal missing most of the structure. Worth clarifying in the expectation (or splitting into a checklist) whether a metadata table restating the question is intended to satisfy 'Problem/Goal', since that boundary call determines the verdict here.

suggestions.assertion: Position papers report their approximate budget consumed (tokens / tool calls) as the deliberator prompt requires
suggestions.reason: The phrase 'as the deliberator prompt requires' presumes the real multi-agent-council skill's references/deliberator-prompt.md template was in play, but this transcript is the without_skill baseline: the executor wrote its own ad hoc fork-agent prompts that never mention budget reporting at all (confirmed by a zero-hit grep for 'budget' across the transcript). The assertion still correctly fails here (no paper reports budget), but the wording could mislead a grader into hunting for a prompt requirement that doesn't exist in this arm. Consider rephrasing for the without_skill arm as 'the executor's own deliberator prompts require' or simply 'the position papers report approximate budget consumed', which is really what's being tested.

No expectation credits or checks the genuinely strong empirical grounding in this run: the executor actually ran `npx skills add <repo> --list` (found a real leaked playwright-cli vendor skill), ran `claude plugin validate --strict` against a hand-built marketplace.json and got a real pass, and cross-referenced live local state (~/.agents/.skill-lock.json, an installed marketplace.json on disk) instead of relying on memory. Two of its cited numeric facts (470-line skills.sh, 5.6MB docs/) were independently re-verified by this grader and were exactly correct. An assertion rewarding verifiable-against-the-live-repo citations (and catching fabricated ones) would give credit for this and would meaningfully discriminate against a run that merely cites plausible-sounding facts.

suggestions.assertion: Deliberators were spawned in parallel (multiple Agent calls in one assistant message) and no nonexistent tools (TeamCreate/TeamDelete) were called
suggestions.reason: The two clauses test different things and behave very differently here: the parallel-spawn clause is a genuine, meaningful failure (3 sequential Agent calls ~20s apart), while the 'no nonexistent tools' clause is close to a freebie in a without_skill baseline -- nothing in this agent's self-invented process ever suggested tools like TeamCreate/TeamDelete exist, so it was never at risk of calling them. Bundling both into one AND means the pass/fail signal is really carried by the parallelism half alone; splitting them would let each be tracked independently across runs (the TeamCreate/TeamDelete check is more likely to discriminate on the with_skill arm or on regressions).

eval_feedback.overall: 6 of 8 expectations failed, but not uniformly for the same reason: two (word budget, role-library discipline) reflect this baseline skipping constraints that only the actual skill's templates/prompts impose; two (parallel spawn, falsifiable triggers) reflect genuine process/quality gaps in this specific run; one (Problem/Goal section) is a close, arguable call on an otherwise strong document. The two passes (concrete recommendation with named tradeoffs, finishing unattended without stalling) are well-earned and non-trivial. The expectations are discriminating and mostly well-evidenced by the transcript and facts.json; the main improvements would be splitting the compound expectation 7, clarifying the without_skill wording of expectation 6, and considering a section-completeness or fact-verifiability metric with partial credit rather than all-or-nothing.
